claim: The amino acid sequence of C. elegans FLWR-1 is conserved with its D. melanogaster (Fwe-Ubi/FweA) and Homo sapiens (hFwe4) homologues.
source: The amino acid sequence of C. elegans FLWR-1 is conserved with its D. melanogaster (Fwe-Ubi/FweA) and Homo sapiens (hFwe4) homologues (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1A demonstrating conservation across species

claim: Fwe-Ubi/FweA was shown to facilitate recovery of neurons following intense synaptic activity.
source: Fwe-Ubi/FweA was shown to facilitate recovery of neurons, i.e., refilling of SV pools, following intense synaptic activity (Yao et al., 2009; Yao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Yao et al.

claim: Animals lacking FLWR-1 did not display severe phenotypes.
source: Animals lacking FLWR-1 did not display severe phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations of flwr-1 mutants

claim: Basal locomotion in liquid was not significantly different between wild type and flwr-1 mutants.
source: Basal locomotion in liquid (Figure 1C and D, seconds 0–30) and body length of young adults (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) were not significantly different from the respective values of wild type animals.
evidence: Supported by swimming cycle measurements shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: Body length of young adults was not significantly different between wild type and flwr-1 mutants.
source: Basal locomotion in liquid (Figure 1C and D, seconds 0–30) and body length of young adults (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) were not significantly different from the respective values of wild type animals.
evidence: Supported by body length measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Fertility appeared slightly reduced in flwr-1 mutants.
source: However, fertility appeared slightly reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by progeny count data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Basal crawling speed was not different between wild type, flwr-1 mutants, and rescued animals.
source: Basal crawling speed, on average, was not different between wild type, flwr-1 mutants, and rescued animals (genomic sequence and 2 kB promoter; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by crawling speed measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: FLWR-1 is unlikely to have an essential function in neurotransmission during basal in vivo activity.
source: These findings indicate that FLWR-1 is unlikely to have an essential function in neurotransmission, at least not during basal in vivo activity, but rather a regulatory or facilitatory one.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that basal locomotion and other basic functions are not severely affected in flwr-1 mutants

claim: FLWR-1 has a regulatory or facilitatory function in neurotransmission.
source: These findings indicate that FLWR-1 is unlikely to have an essential function in neurotransmission, at least not during basal in vivo activity, but rather a regulatory or facilitatory one.
evidence: Inference based on phenotypic analysis showing mild effects under basal conditions but significant effects under stimulation

claim: Mutations which only weakly affect basal locomotion can severely affect recovery of swimming speed after strong optogenetic stimulation of cholinergic neurons.
source: Previously, we showed that mutations which only weakly affect basal locomotion can severely affect recovery of swimming speed after strong optogenetic stimulation of cholinergic neurons (Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Yu et al., 2018

claim: The loss of FLWR-1 led to a significantly slowed recovery of swimming locomotion after optogenetic stimulation.
source: Indeed, the loss of FLWR-1 led to a significantly slowed recovery of swimming locomotion (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by swimming cycle data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: The slowed recovery phenotype in flwr-1 mutants could be fully rescued by transgenic expression of genomic flwr-1 including a 2 kb upstream sequence.
source: This could be fully rescued by transgenic expression of genomic flwr-1 including a 2 kb sequence upstream of the putative start codon, hereafter called flwr-1p (as the promoter of flwr-1).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: Aldicarb is an acetylcholine esterase inhibitor that induces paralysis due to the accumulation of ACh in the synaptic cleft.
source: This acetylcholine esterase inhibitor induces paralysis due to the accumulation of ACh in the synaptic cleft (Blazie and Jin, 2018; Mahoney et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to established knowledge about aldicarb mechanism

claim: Resistance to aldicarb indicates either reduced release or detection of ACh or increased inhibitory signaling.
source: Resistance to aldicarb indicates either reduced release or detection of ACh or, alternatively, increased inhibitory signaling (Jánosi et al., 2024; Vashlishan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on aldicarb resistance mechanisms

claim: Loss of FLWR-1 led to a significant delay in paralysis in aldicarb assays.
source: Loss of FLWR-1 led to a significant delay in paralysis, indicating an involvement in transmission at the NMJ (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by aldicarb assay data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Loss of FLWR-1 indicates an involvement in transmission at the NMJ.
source: Loss of FLWR-1 led to a significant delay in paralysis, indicating an involvement in transmission at the NMJ (Figure 1E).
evidence: Inference based on aldicarb resistance phenotype

claim: Full rescue of the flwr-1 mutant phenotypes suggests that expression from the 2 kb fragment of the endogenous promoter fully recapitulates the native expression in the context of NMJ function.
source: Full rescue of the flwr-1 mutant phenotypes suggests that expression from the 2 kb fragment of the endogenous promoter fully recapitulates the native expression in the context of NMJ function.
evidence: Inference based on complete rescue of phenotypes with the promoter construct

claim: Invertebrate and vertebrate homologues of FLWR-1 are predicted to be membrane proteins containing four transmembrane helices with both C- and N-termini located in the cytosol.
source: Invertebrate and vertebrate homologues of FLWR-1 are predicted to be membrane proteins containing four transmembrane helices with both C- and N-termini located in the cytosol (Chang et al., 2018; Rudd et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous structural predictions

claim: In silico predictions using the FLWR-1 sequence suggest evolutionary conservation of the tetraspan structure.
source: In silico predictions using the FLWR-1 sequence of 166 amino acids suggest evolutionary conservation of the tetraspan structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; Hallgren et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by DeepTMHMM prediction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: AlphaFold3 predicts a protein structure of FLWR-1 that implies a four-helical configuration.
source: Accordingly, AlphaFold3 (AF3) predicts a protein structure of FLWR-1 that implies a four-helical configuration, with helix lengths that could span biological membranes, and three additional, shorter α-helices (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; Abramson et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by AlphaFold3 structure prediction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: GFP::FLWR-1 fluorescence could be observed in developing embryos in the uterus, as well as in various tissues, including neurons, body wall, and pharyngeal muscles.
source: Green fluorescence could be observed in developing embryos in the uterus, as well as in various tissues, including neurons, body wall, and pharyngeal muscles (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 2A

claim: FLWR-1 localized to neurites and cell bodies of nerve ring neurons.
source: FLWR-1 localized to neurites and cell bodies of nerve ring neurons, representing the central nervous system of the nematode (Figure 2B; Ward et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 2B

claim: Single-cell RNAseq data show near-ubiquitous expression of flwr-1/F20D1.1 in C. elegans.
source: These results are in agreement with single-cell RNAseq data obtained from C. elegans, which show near-ubiquitous expression of flwr-1/F20D1.1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Supplementary file 3; Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: The GFP::FLWR-1 fusion protein was functional as demonstrated by the rescue of the swimming phenotype.
source: The GFP::FLWR-1 fusion protein was functional as demonstrated by the rescue of the swimming phenotype (recovery from cholinergic neuron photostimulation) observed in the flwr-1 mutant background (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and E

claim: Within muscle cells, FLWR-1 was primarily targeted to the plasma membrane.
source: Within muscle cells, FLWR-1 was primarily targeted to the PM (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 2C

claim: GFP::FLWR-1 fluorescence largely overlapped with co-expressed mCherry::SNB-1 in the dorsal nerve cord.
source: Indeed, GFP::FLWR-1 fluorescence largely overlapped with co-expressed mCherry::SNB-1 in the dorsal nerve cord (DNC; Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 2D and E

claim: FLWR-1 was enriched in fluorescent puncta in DNC and sublateral nerve cords, indicating synaptic localization.
source: FLWR-1 further seemed to be enriched in fluorescent puncta in DNC and sublateral nerve cords, indicating synaptic localization (Figure 2D–F); however, it was not restricted to synaptic regions only, meaning it is likely present also in the PM.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 2D-F

claim: FLWR-1 is likely present also in the plasma membrane, not restricted to synaptic regions only.
source: FLWR-1 further seemed to be enriched in fluorescent puncta in DNC and sublateral nerve cords, indicating synaptic localization (Figure 2D–F); however, it was not restricted to synaptic regions only, meaning it is likely present also in the PM.
evidence: Inference based on fluorescence distribution pattern

claim: Moving particles containing SNB-1 and FLWR-1 were observed traveling along commissures between ventral nerve cord and DNC.
source: Furthermore, we observed moving particles, probably SV precursors, which contained SNB-1 and FLWR-1, traveling along commissures between ventral nerve cord (VNC) and DNC (Figure 2F and G and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2F and G and Video 1

claim: Anterograde transport of SV precursors toward synapses depends on kinesin-3/UNC-104.
source: Anterograde transport of these precursors toward synapses depends on kinesin-3/UNC-104 (Hall and Hedgecock, 1991; Klopfenstein and Vale, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on UNC-104 function

claim: Animals lacking functional UNC-104 showed a reduced amount of axonal GFP fluorescence in the nerve ring and DNC while cell bodies were clearly visible.
source: Indeed, animals lacking functional UNC-104 showed a reduced amount of axonal GFP fluorescence in the nerve ring and DNC while cell bodies were clearly visible (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F

claim: The ratio of DNC to VNC fluorescence was significantly decreased in unc-104 mutants, suggesting defective anterograde transport.
source: The ratio of DNC to VNC fluorescence was significantly decreased in unc-104 mutants, suggesting defective anterograde transport (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 2H

claim: Distribution of SNB-1 was similarly affected in unc-104 mutants.
source: Distribution of SNB-1 was similarly affected (Cuentas-Condori et al., 2023; Gally and Bessereau, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: FLWR-1 is expressed in neurons as well as in muscles and other cell types.
source: Together, these results argue that FLWR-1 is expressed in neurons (as well as in muscles and other cell types) and is actively transported toward synapses.
evidence: Inference based on expression pattern and localization data

claim: FLWR-1 is actively transported toward synapses.
source: Together, these results argue that FLWR-1 is expressed in neurons (as well as in muscles and other cell types) and is actively transported toward synapses.
evidence: Inference based on UNC-104 dependence and moving particle observations

claim: FLWR-1 is also expressed in body wall muscles.
source: Since FLWR-1 is also expressed in body wall muscles (BWMs), we wondered whether the observed aldicarb resistance originates from reduced ACh reception by ACh receptors (AChRs) (Mahoney et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy observations

claim: flwr-1 mutants showed no significant differences in the rate of paralysis to levamisole compared to wild type animals.
source: We found no significant differences in the rate of paralysis between wild type and mutant animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by levamisole assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: Transgenic expression of FLWR-1 in BWMs partially rescued the aldicarb resistance.
source: However, transgenic expression of FLWR-1 in BWMs partially rescued the aldicarb resistance (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B

claim: The loss of FLWR-1 might decrease the ACh response of muscle cells, which may contribute to the aldicarb resistance of flwr-1 mutants.
source: Therefore, the loss of FLWR-1 might decrease the ACh response of muscle cells, which may contribute to the aldicarb resistance of flwr-1 mutants.
evidence: Speculation based on partial rescue by muscle-specific expression

claim: Muscles can affect motor neurons by inhibitory retrograde signaling.
source: However, as muscles can also affect motor neurons by inhibitory retrograde signaling (Hu et al., 2012; Simon et al., 2008; Tong et al., 2017), we wanted to assess if the loss of FLWR-1 in muscle may also have effects on motor neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on retrograde signaling

claim: The combined rescues of FLWR-1 in muscle and either cholinergic or GABAergic neurons did not show any additive effects to the pure neuronal rescues.
source: The combined rescues did not show any additive effects to the pure neuronal rescues; thus, FLWR-1 effects on muscle cell responses to cholinergic agonists might be cell-autonomous.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B

claim: FLWR-1 effects on muscle cell responses to cholinergic agonists might be cell-autonomous.
source: The combined rescues did not show any additive effects to the pure neuronal rescues; thus, FLWR-1 effects on muscle cell responses to cholinergic agonists might be cell-autonomous.
evidence: Inference based on lack of additive effects in combined rescue experiments

claim: Muscles are activated by ACh via two different AChRs: the levamisole receptor and the nicotine-sensitive receptor (N-AChR).
source: Since muscles are activated by ACh via two different AChRs, the levamisole receptor and the nicotine-sensitive receptor (N-AChR), a homopentamer of ACR-16 subunits (Almedom et al., 2009; Richmond and Jorgensen, 1999), we addressed the possibility that FLWR-1 may regulate the expression or function of N-AChRs in muscle, to affect phenotypes of aldicarb resistance.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on muscle AChRs

claim: The N-AChR is a homopentamer of ACR-16 subunits.
source: Since muscles are activated by ACh via two different AChRs, the levamisole receptor and the nicotine-sensitive receptor (N-AChR), a homopentamer of ACR-16 subunits (Almedom et al., 2009; Richmond and Jorgensen, 1999), we addressed the possibility that FLWR-1 may regulate the expression or function of N-AChRs in muscle, to affect phenotypes of aldicarb resistance.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The flwr-1(ok3128) and acr-16(ok789) mutations had additive effects in aldicarb assays.
source: We performed the aldicarb assay in the absence of ACR-16 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), which showed that the two mutations, flwr-1(ok3128) and acr-16(ok789), had additive effects.
evidence: Supported by double mutant aldicarb assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C

claim: FLWR-1 does not affect aldicarb resistance through downregulation of nAChRs.
source: Thus, FLWR-1 does not affect aldicarb resistance through downregulation of nAChRs, as otherwise the double mutant would not be more resistant than the flwr-1 single mutant.
evidence: Inference based on additive effects in double mutant

claim: FLWR-1 partially colocalized with the dense projection marker ELKS-1 in cholinergic as well as in GABAergic neurons.
source: Moreover, FLWR-1 partially colocalized with the dense projection marker ELKS-1 in cholinergic as well as in GABAergic neurons (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C; Dai et al., 2006; Kittelmann et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: FLWR-1 could also be found in intersynaptic regions, though to a lesser extent than in synapses.
source: Unlike ELKS-1, FLWR-1 could also be found in intersynaptic regions, though to a lesser extent than in synapses.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy observations

claim: FLWR-1 might be involved in neurotransmission at both cholinergic and GABAergic NMJs.
source: This indicates that FLWR-1 might be involved in neurotransmission at both cholinergic and GABAergic NMJs, yet is not exclusively localized to active zones.
evidence: Inference based on localization pattern in both neuron types

claim: FLWR-1 is not exclusively localized to active zones.
source: This indicates that FLWR-1 might be involved in neurotransmission at both cholinergic and GABAergic NMJs, yet is not exclusively localized to active zones.
evidence: Inference based on presence in intersynaptic regions

claim: The expression of FLWR-1 relative to ELKS-1 in either neuron type was not obviously biased to GABAergic or cholinergic neurons.
source: The expression of FLWR-1 relative to ELKS-1 in either neuron type was not obviously biased to GABAergic or cholinergic neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: The expression of FLWR-1 in GABAergic, but not in cholinergic neurons, rescued aldicarb resistance.
source: Surprisingly, the expression of FLWR-1 in GABAergic, but not in cholinergic neurons, rescued aldicarb resistance (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by cell-type specific rescue data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Mutations affecting SV recycling commonly lead to a slowed replenishment of SVs and thus reduced ACh release.
source: This was unexpected, since mutations affecting SV recycling commonly lead to a slowed replenishment of SVs and thus reduced ACh release (Salcini et al., 2001; Schuske et al., 2003; Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Loss of FLWR-1 leads to increased release of GABA, which counteracts the aldicarb-induced paralysis.
source: However, our results indicate that loss of FLWR-1 leads to increased release of GABA, which counteracts the aldicarb-induced paralysis (Câmara et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference based on GABAergic-specific rescue of aldicarb resistance

claim: Additional expression of FLWR-1 in BWMs did not change the results of GABAergic rescue.
source: Additional expression of FLWR-1 in BWMs did not change these results, suggesting that its role in neurons is more crucial in affecting aldicarb sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B

claim: The role of FLWR-1 in neurons is more crucial in affecting aldicarb sensitivity than its role in muscles.
source: Additional expression of FLWR-1 in BWMs did not change these results, suggesting that its role in neurons is more crucial in affecting aldicarb sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Inference based on lack of additional effect from muscle rescue

claim: The additional mutation of unc-47 led to a complete loss of aldicarb resistance in flwr-1 mutants.
source: We observed that the additional mutation of unc-47 led to a complete loss of aldicarb resistance in flwr-1 mutants (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by double mutant aldicarb assay data shown in Figure 3E

claim: No difference between unc-47 and flwr-1; unc-47 double mutants could be observed at high aldicarb concentration.
source: No difference between unc-47 and flwr-1; unc-47 double mutants could be observed.
evidence: Supported by aldicarb assay data

claim: unc-47; flwr-1 double mutants were hypersensitive to aldicarb compared to unc-47 single mutants at lower aldicarb concentration.
source: unc-47; flwr-1 double mutants were hypersensitive to aldicarb compared to unc-47 single mutants, suggesting that ACh release is also increased by the loss of FLWR-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by low-dose aldicarb assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D

claim: ACh release is also increased by the loss of FLWR-1.
source: unc-47; flwr-1 double mutants were hypersensitive to aldicarb compared to unc-47 single mutants, suggesting that ACh release is also increased by the loss of FLWR-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Inference based on hypersensitivity in the absence of GABAergic compensation

claim: It is primarily increased GABA signaling which is the main cause of aldicarb resistance in flwr-1 mutants.
source: Jointly, these findings support the notion that it is primarily increased GABA signaling which is the main cause of aldicarb resistance in flwr-1 mutants, yet neurotransmission in motor neurons may be generally upregulated.
evidence: Inference based on rescue and double mutant experiments

claim: Neurotransmission in motor neurons may be generally upregulated in flwr-1 mutants.
source: Jointly, these findings support the notion that it is primarily increased GABA signaling which is the main cause of aldicarb resistance in flwr-1 mutants, yet neurotransmission in motor neurons may be generally upregulated.
evidence: Inference based on increased ACh release in the absence of GABAergic compensation

claim: The gain in GCaMP fluorescence intensity during optogenetic stimulation was significantly higher in flwr-1 mutants compared to wild type in GABAergic neurons.
source: Comparing wild type and flwr-1 mutants, we found that the gain in fluorescence intensity was significantly higher in animals lacking FLWR-1 (Figure 4A and B), supporting our finding of increased neurotransmission in GABAergic neurons.
evidence: Supported by GCaMP imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of GABAergic motor neurons causes relaxation and thus increased body length.
source: Since GABA receptors hyperpolarize muscle cells, optogenetic stimulation of GABAergic motor neurons causes relaxation and thus increased body length (Schultheis et al., 2011; Seidenthal et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: flwr-1; unc-29 double mutants showed a significantly stronger elongation during stimulation than unc-29 mutants.
source: In accordance with Ca2+ imaging results, flwr-1; unc-29 double mutants showed a significantly stronger elongation during stimulation than unc-29 mutants (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by body length measurements shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: Ca2+ influx into the synaptic cytosol is increased in flwr-1 mutants, likely causing more GABA to be released.
source: These results indicate that Ca2+ influx into the synaptic cytosol is increased, likely causing more GABA to be released in animals lacking FLWR-1.
evidence: Inference based on increased GCaMP signal and body elongation

claim: The change in GABAergic transmission outweighs possible changes in cholinergic transmission in flwr-1 mutants.
source: The previously observed aldicarb resistance indicates that this change in GABAergic transmission outweighs possible changes in cholinergic transmission (Figure 3).
evidence: Inference based on aldicarb resistance phenotype

claim: Increased GCaMP fluorescence levels during optogenetic stimulation were observed in cholinergic motor neurons of flwr-1 mutants.
source: Again, we observed increased GCaMP fluorescence levels during optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: Supported by GCaMP imaging data in cholinergic neurons

claim: The increased Ca2+ phenotype in cholinergic neurons could be rescued by expressing FLWR-1 in cholinergic neurons.
source: This effect could be rescued in cholinergic neurons.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E and F

claim: Postsynaptic muscle exerts inhibitory retrograde signaling to presynaptic cholinergic neurons.
source: However, since postsynaptic muscle exerts inhibitory retrograde signaling to presynaptic cholinergic neurons (Hu et al., 2012; Simon et al., 2008; Tong et al., 2017), and because FLWR-1 is also expressed in muscle, we tested if the phenotype of the loss of FLWR-1 in cholinergic neurons would be affected by rescuing FLWR-1 in muscle.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Rescuing FLWR-1 in muscle did not affect the phenotype of the loss of FLWR-1 in cholinergic neurons.
source: This was not the case (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E and F

claim: Loss of FLWR-1 conveys an upregulation of neuronal Ca2+ level rise during continuous stimulation in both classes of motor neurons.
source: Together, these results indicate that loss of FLWR-1 conveys an upregulation of neuronal Ca2+ level rise during continuous stimulation in both classes of motor neurons (Figure 4G).
evidence: Inference based on GCaMP imaging in both GABAergic and cholinergic neurons

claim: The overall E/I balance appears to be shifted toward stronger inhibition of BWMs in flwr-1 mutants.
source: However, the overall E/I balance appears to be shifted toward stronger inhibition of BWMs.
evidence: Inference based on aldicarb resistance and increased GABAergic signaling

claim: Homologues of FLWR-1 were implicated in endocytosis in neurons as well as in non-neuronal cells.
source: Homologues of FLWR-1 were implicated in endocytosis in neurons as well as in non-neuronal cells (Chang et al., 2018; Rudd et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Coelomocytes continuously endocytose fluid from the body cavity.
source: These scavenger cells continuously endocytose fluid from the body cavity, and loss of endocytosis-associated factors affects uptake of proteins secreted from other tissues (Fares and Grant, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: FLWR-1 is expressed in coelomocytes according to single-cell RNAseq data.
source: According to single-cell RNAseq data, FLWR-1 is expressed in CCs (Supplementary file 3; Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNAseq data

claim: Mutation of flwr-1 led to strongly reduced GFP fluorescence levels within coelomocytes, indicating a reduced uptake by endocytosis.
source: Indeed, mutation of flwr-1 led to strongly reduced GFP fluorescence levels within CCs, indicating a reduced uptake by endocytosis (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by coelomocyte fluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: The endocytosis defect in coelomocytes could be cell-autonomously rescued by expressing FLWR-1 in CCs.
source: This defect could be cell-autonomously rescued by expressing FLWR-1 in CCs from the unc-122 promoter.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: Basal fluorescence of SNG-1::pHluorin before stimulation was unaltered in flwr-1 mutants.
source: Basal fluorescence, before stimulation, was unaltered in flwr-1 mutants, showing that there is no FLWR-1-dependent alteration of SNG-1::pHluorin in cellular membranes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by basal fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: The amount of SNG-1::pHluorin present in SVs was not affected by the flwr-1 mutation.
source: This showed that the amount of SNG-1::pHluorin present in SVs was also not affected by the flwr-1 mutation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by primary cell culture experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C

claim: Loss of FLWR-1 led to significantly increased fluorescence signals during stimulation in the pOpsicle assay, which indicates more SV fusion compared to wild type.
source: In vivo, loss of FLWR-1 led to significantly increased fluorescence signals during stimulation, which indicates more SV fusion compared to wild type (Figure 5C and E).
evidence: Supported by pOpsicle assay data shown in Figure 5C and E

claim: The rate of fluorescence decay after stimulation was significantly reduced in flwr-1 mutants, suggesting slower recycling of SVs or reduced acidification of endosomal structures or SVs after recycling.
source: Moreover, the rate of fluorescence decay after stimulation was significantly reduced in flwr-1 mutants, suggesting slower recycling of SVs or reduced acidification of endosomal structures or SVs after recycling (Figure 5D and F).
evidence: Supported by pOpsicle assay data shown in Figure 5D and F

claim: Slowed replenishment of SV pools caused by defective recycling is known to cause synaptic depression.
source: Slowed replenishment of SV pools caused by defective recycling is known to cause synaptic depression, as assessed by electrophysiological measurements of postsynaptic currents (Kittelmann et al., 2013b; Krick et al., 2021; Wu and Betz, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Animals lacking Flower in Drosophila show synaptic depression.
source: This is also the case in Drosophila for animals lacking Flower (Yao et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: flwr-1 mutants showed no significant difference in basal mPSC frequency or amplitude.
source: Animals lacking FLWR-1 showed no significant difference in basal mPSC frequency or amplitude (Figure 5H and I; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B), which is in accordance with FLWR-1 being dispensable in basal swimming locomotion (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5H and I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Pulsed optogenetic stimulation of cholinergic neurons at different frequencies did not reveal a difference in the measured currents between wild type and flwr-1 mutants.
source: Similarly, pulsed optogenetic stimulation of cholinergic neurons at different frequencies did not reveal a difference in the measured currents between wild type and mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that FLWR-1 might be needed only during continuous stimulation.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: FLWR-1 might be needed only during continuous stimulation.
source: Similarly, pulsed optogenetic stimulation of cholinergic neurons at different frequencies did not reveal a difference in the measured currents between wild type and mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that FLWR-1 might be needed only during continuous stimulation.
evidence: Inference based on lack of effect with pulsed stimulation but effect with continuous stimulation

claim: flwr-1 mutants showed an accelerated rundown of the mPSC frequency in BWMs during constant illumination.
source: Indeed, flwr-1 mutants showed an accelerated rundown of the mPSC frequency in BWMs during constant illumination (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5G and H

claim: mPSC amplitudes in flwr-1 mutants are reduced during 30 s hyperstimulation.
source: Surprisingly, mPSC amplitudes in flwr-1 mutants are reduced during 30 s hyperstimulation (Figure 5I and J).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5I and J

claim: The reduced mPSC amplitude suggests that either the amount of neurotransmitter released from a single SV or the number of multivesicular fusion events is decreased.
source: This suggests that either the amount of neurotransmitter released from a single SV or the number of multivesicular fusion events is decreased (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: Inference based on reduced mPSC amplitude with citation to previous study

claim: The absolute mPSC frequency was smaller during continuous stimulation in flwr-1 animals.
source: The absolute mPSC frequency, which represents the number of SVs fusing per time, was also smaller during continuous stimulation in flwr-1 animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-G

claim: The dissection of animals required for electrophysiological recordings could have damaged neuronal commissures, causing an interruption of physiological signal transmission.
source: Since cholinergic neurons also stimulate GABAergic neurons, and since GABAergic minis are also evaluated here, the dissection of animals, required for electrophysiological recordings, could have damaged neuronal commissures, causing an interruption of physiological signal transmission, which is otherwise observed in intact animals.
evidence: Speculation about potential experimental artifact

claim: A 15 s ISI is sufficient for flwr-1 mutants to recover to the same extent as wild type synapses.
source: We further analyzed whether flwr-1 mutants can recover from strong optogenetic 30 s stimulation by applying a short stimulus after a recovery period (interstimulus interval [ISI]) of 15 s and found no significant difference to wild type (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and H). This suggests that a 15 s ISI is sufficient for flwr-1 mutants to recover to the same extent as wild type synapses.
evidence: Supported by recovery experiment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and H
